title: Design a Key-Value Store
subtitle: Build a Dynamo-style store that stays writable when nodes die, and watch a key travel through the ring, quorums, gossip and hinted handoff.
learn: How consistent hashing with virtual nodes spreads keys and limits data movement
How N, R and W set the trade-off between latency, durability and freshness
How gossip lets nodes agree on who is alive without a central master
How hinted handoff keeps writes accepted while a replica is down
How vector clocks detect concurrent writes that must be reconciled

steps.title: A store that never says no
steps.body: Design a key-value store (think "look up a value by its name") for a shopping cart. It must handle 200,000 operations per second and 50 TB of data, with values under 10 KB. It must also accept writes when machines fail or a data centre link breaks. One database server is a poor fit: it would be a single point of failure and has no headroom for that load. So the data must be split across many nodes (servers). The hard part is that any node can fail at any time, and we still want fast answers.
steps.idea: Choose availability and low latency up front, and accept that replicas may briefly disagree.
steps.caption: A client talks to a cluster of nodes, not to one server.

steps.title: Place the key on a ring
steps.body: First, which node owns which key? Hash the key (say cart:42) to a point on a ring of hash values. Each node owns many points on the ring, called virtual nodes (often 16 to 256 per machine). The key belongs to the first node clockwise from its point. When a node is added, it takes small slices from many neighbours, so only about 1/N of keys move, instead of nearly all of them. Any node can act as the coordinator, the node that handles a request and finds the owners.
steps.idea: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes spreads load evenly and keeps rebalancing cheap.
steps.caption: The client sends PUT cart:42; the coordinator hashes the key onto the ring.

steps.title: Copy it to N nodes
steps.body: One copy would be lost with its machine. So the coordinator writes to the key's owner plus the next distinct nodes on the ring, giving N = 3 replicas (copies), ideally in different racks or zones. Every node has the full ring map, so the coordinator sends the write straight to all three, with no lookup service in the middle. N = 3 is a rule of thumb: no data is lost unless all three copies die, at three times the storage.
steps.idea: Replication is what makes failure survivable; the ring tells you which nodes hold a key.
steps.caption: The coordinator sends the write to three replicas.

steps.title: Wait for W acknowledgements
steps.body: Waiting for all three replicas would make every write as slow as the slowest node. Instead, the coordinator answers the client after W = 2 acknowledgements (acks). Assume 1 ms network time, replicas that need 2 to 3 ms to save, and one replica frozen for 40 ms by a garbage-collection pause (the runtime briefly stops to clean memory). The write finishes in about 4 ms, not 40. The slow third replica still gets the data.
steps.idea: A write quorum W hides slow replicas: latency is set by the W-th fastest, not the slowest.
steps.caption: Two acks arrive, so the client is answered while C is still stuck.

steps.title: Read R, overlap with W
steps.body: A read asks the replicas and waits for R = 2 answers. Because R + W = 4 is greater than N = 3, any two replicas that answer must include at least one that acknowledged the latest write (when writes went to the key's home replicas). The coordinator returns the newest value (judged by a vector clock, explained later) in about 3 ms, and quietly fixes stale replicas in the background (read repair). Setting R = 1 reads faster but may return old data.
steps.idea: When R + W > N and writes go to the key's home replicas, the read set overlaps the write set, so reads normally see the latest acknowledged write.
steps.caption: Two replicas answer, and the overlap with the write set carries the newest value.

steps.title: Detecting failure without a master
steps.body: Nodes need to know who is alive and who owns which ring slices. Every second, each node picks a random peer and swaps what it knows: the member list, heartbeat counters (numbers each node keeps raising to prove it is alive) and ring changes. News reaches everyone in roughly log2(cluster size) rounds, so a 1,000-node cluster agrees in about 10 to 15 seconds. A node marks a peer "suspect" when its heartbeat has not advanced for a while. No central master exists to fail or become a bottleneck.
steps.idea: Gossip spreads membership and failure information epidemically, with no single point of failure.
steps.caption: Peers swap heartbeat tables with random neighbours.

steps.title: A replica dies mid-write
steps.body: Node C crashes. The write for cart:42 still reaches A and B, which both ack, so W = 2 is met and the client sees success in about 4 ms. If a second replica were also down, a strict quorum would reject the write. Dynamo-style stores relax this with a sloppy quorum: a healthy stand-in node may take the write instead. That keeps writes available but weakens the "reads overlap writes" guarantee until the missed data is replayed.
steps.idea: With N = 3 and W = 2 the system tolerates one failed replica with no client-visible effect.
steps.caption: C is unreachable, but A and B still acknowledge.

steps.title: Hinted handoff
steps.body: To keep three copies alive, the coordinator also sends C's copy to node D, the next healthy node on the ring, with a hint: "this belongs to C". D's ack means three copies exist (A, B and D), but C still has none. D keeps hints in a separate area. When gossip reports that C is back, D sends the hinted writes to C and deletes them. Hints are kept for a limited outage window, for example 3 hours. A slower background repair, anti-entropy using Merkle trees (hash trees that find which key ranges differ), fixes any remaining gap.
steps.idea: Hinted handoff catches a returning node up quickly; anti-entropy repair is the safety net.
steps.caption: D holds C's write with a hint, then forwards it when C returns.

steps.title: Concurrent writes and vector clocks
steps.body: Two phones update the same cart at the same moment, through different coordinators (in the diagram, A and B each play coordinator), so neither sees the other's write. Each coordinator stamps its write with a vector clock: a list of (node, counter) pairs, here [A:1] and [B:1]. Neither clock includes the other, so the writes are concurrent, and the store keeps both as siblings. Replicas swap versions so each holds both. The next read returns both, the app merges them (for example, the union of the two carts), and it writes the result back with a clock covering both.
steps.idea: Vector clocks tell causal order from true concurrency; concurrent versions are kept and merged, not silently dropped.
steps.caption: Two concurrent versions are stored side by side as siblings.

steps.title: The whole design
steps.body: A hash ring places each key on N = 3 replicas. Quorums W = 2 and R = 2 give fast reads and writes that overlap. Gossip finds failures, hinted handoff and Merkle-tree repair heal them, and vector clocks expose conflicts for the application to merge. The price is eventual consistency (replicas may briefly disagree, then converge). If you need strict single-copy ordering, use a consensus-based store instead.
steps.idea: Dynamo-style systems trade strict consistency for availability, using tunable quorums to choose the balance.
steps.caption: Every mechanism serves one goal: stay writable.

quiz.q: A cluster has 10 nodes with virtual nodes and you add an 11th. Roughly what share of keys must move?
options: About 100%, because the hash modulus changed
About 50%
About 1/11 of the keys, taken in small slices from many nodes
None; new nodes only take new keys
quiz.why: Consistent hashing only reassigns the slices the new node takes over, roughly 1/N of the data, and virtual nodes spread that load across many donors.

quiz.q: With N = 3 you choose W = 1 and R = 1. What is the main risk?
options: Writes become very slow
The ring cannot be built
Vector clocks stop working
A read can hit a replica that has not received the latest write
quiz.why: R + W = 2 is not greater than N = 3, so the read set and write set may not overlap, and stale reads are possible.

quiz.q: Replica C is down and a write uses N = 3, W = 2. Which statement is correct?
options: It succeeds with A and B; a hint can later bring C up to date
The write must fail until C returns
The coordinator must elect a leader first
Both A and B must be rolled back
quiz.why: Two acks meet W, so the write succeeds. A stand-in node can hold a hint and replay it to C when gossip shows C is back.

quiz.q: Two clients write the same key at the same time via different coordinators. Their vector clocks are [A:1] and [B:1]. In a Dynamo-style store that never silently drops concurrent updates, what should the store do?
options: Keep the one with the later wall-clock timestamp and discard the other
Reject the second write
Keep both as siblings and let a later read reconcile them
Pick the lower node id
quiz.why: Neither clock descends from the other, so the writes are concurrent. Dropping one by timestamp can lose data; keeping siblings lets the application merge.

quiz.q: Why do nodes use gossip rather than one health-check master?
options: Gossip is always faster than a master
A master is a single point of failure and bottleneck; gossip spreads information through random peer exchanges
Gossip guarantees strong consistency
A master makes strong consistency impossible
quiz.why: Gossip needs no special node, scales with cluster size, and still converges in about log N rounds, though a view may be briefly stale.

cheatsheet.def: Maps keys and nodes onto a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys.
Each machine owns many small ring slices (commonly 16 to 256 depending on the system), giving even load and letting bigger machines take more slices.
N replicas per key; reads wait for R answers, writes wait for W acks. R + W > N makes reads overlap the latest write.
When a home replica is down, a write may be accepted by another healthy node so the write still reaches W nodes.
A stand-in node stores a write meant for a down node, with a hint, and replays it once that node is back.
Per-node counters attached to a value. If one clock includes another, it is newer; if neither does, the writes are concurrent.
Read repair fixes stale replicas seen during reads. Anti-entropy compares Merkle trees in the background to fix the rest.
Nodes periodically swap state with random peers, so membership and failure news spreads to everyone in about log N rounds.

lab.prompt: Design the key-value store for a cart service: 200,000 operations per second at peak (70% reads), 20 billion keys, average value 2 KB, always writable, and surviving the loss of one availability zone out of three. Choose partitioning, replication, quorum settings, failure handling and conflict handling, and justify each with numbers.
requirements: Estimate raw data size and total size with replication, then the node count if one node holds 4 TB
State N, R and W and explain which failures and staleness they allow
Explain how keys map to nodes and how adding a node limits data movement
Describe how a write behaves when one replica is down, including hinted handoff
Describe how failure detection and membership spread without a master
Explain how concurrent writes are detected and who resolves them
Describe a repair path for data a hint did not cover
hints: 20 billion keys times 2 KB is about 40 TB before replication; multiply by N
Spread the three replicas across the three zones so a zone loss removes one copy
If R + W > N and writes reach the home replicas, a quorum read normally sees the latest acked write; sloppy quorums and hints weaken this
Carts merge by union (deleted items may reappear unless removals are tracked); counters can use CRDTs; a balance needs conditional or consensus-backed writes
Keep disks under about 50-60% full (compaction, repair need headroom), round nodes to a multiple of 3 for zone balance, and check survivors carry about 1.5x load after losing a zone
Hints expire, so something slower such as Merkle tree comparison must cover long outages
checklist: Storage and node count are computed with replication included
Node count includes headroom and zone balance, and throughput (writes x N, reads x R) is sanity-checked
R + W vs N is stated and its consequence explained
Replicas are placed in different failure domains
A single node failure does not make writes fail
Conflict detection method and merge owner are named
Both short-term (hints) and long-term (anti-entropy) repair are covered
